name: Esther Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a stacker at a large mine, laying crushed ore onto the stockpile without burying the access lane. I am 58 with a vocational certificate, and I know when the belt tracks badly by the smell of hot rubber. I like a neat pile and a clear handover, but dislike finding a jam that the last shift did not report. My partner is a paramedic with steady work, our children are grown, and we have about three months of expenses saved on my usual mine wage. A few other mines are close enough to try if needed, and I use AI every day to search fault logs before walking to the belt to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew faster fault notes could help if every entry still names the person who checked the belt. I would say stockpile work still needs eyes on the ore and a hand near the stop switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the small tools could make my handover clearer without cutting my hours. With my partner's wages and three months saved, a routine breakdown would not threaten the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking the stacker belt at each handover and marking jams in the log. I'd use the AI fault search to compare repeated jams before asking maintenance for parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly settled about this version. A useful search tool is welcome, and our wages leave enough space for a normal repair bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a fault search help you find?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A string of late-shift entries showed the same chute sticking after wet ore came through. I took the pattern to the fitter, who found a bent guide plate. The fitter still had to see the bent guide plate after the AI search found a pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner after that shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the search saved walking through a stack of paper, but the fitter still had to see the plate. We would keep our three-month reserve for trouble that a log cannot solve.

think: I think the small tools could make my **handover clearer** without cutting my hours.

Use the **AI fault search** to compare repeated jams before asking maintenance for parts.
feel: I feel **calm** about my work and pleased by clearer fault records.
S0.quote: The fitter still had to see the bent guide plate after the AI search found a pattern.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** helps her connect fault records, while physical checks remain part of each handover.
Steady partner income and **three months saved** support her calm view of small changes.

steps.text: Keep checking the stacker belt and recording jams
Search AI fault logs for repeated jams before ordering parts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew automated planning may change ore orders before it can clear a jammed stacker. I would ask the union for operator input when new targets are set from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think faster planning could shrink weekend shifts that help us build a retirement cushion. I can learn a new screen, but I want to know whether it quietly makes two belts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union planning meeting and bring the last six weekend rosters. I'd test the new fault dashboard on a paid shift against my own jam log. I'd apply for a maintenance scheduling post if weekend stacker shifts disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be interested in the dashboard and worried about the roster. Losing some weekend pay would not break us, but it would push retirement further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare on the dashboard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check whether it shows the wet-ore jams that happen when the chute is loaded too fast. If those disappear from the report, the target will look easy only on a screen. A target can look easy on a screen after the wet-ore jams disappear from the report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why consider scheduling if AI is improving planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might be a temporary bridge and a way to keep a wage while I look at maintenance work. I would not call a desk job safe once full thinking AI can do planning cheaply.

feel: I feel **anxious about hours** and curious about the new dashboard.
S1.quote: A target can look easy on a screen after the wet-ore jams disappear from the report.
fieldNote: She uses **roster evidence** through the union and tests the dashboard against a known wet-ore problem.
She views **scheduling work** as a temporary bridge and expects strong thinking AI to reach that desk role.

steps.text: Join the union planning meeting with six weekend rosters

Apply for maintenance scheduling if stacker weekends disappear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI by 2028 can plan and inspect logs, but hands-on stacker robots follow around 2031. I would press for a funded transfer before the mine replaces operators at the belt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect robot stackers around 2031 to cut my paid shifts, even if someone still watches the plant. Three months of savings would not bridge years without a wage, and nearby sites may buy the same machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the plant manager this week which stacker tests need human operators. I'd apply for mechanical fitter training if the mine pays fees and keeps my wage. I'd bring a transition demand to the union committee before the next contract meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am alarmed because the change would reach my seat while I am still paying into retirement. I lie awake calculating how quickly three months of savings would go if a course did not lead to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still watch the belt if people are needed until robots arrive around 2031. Full thinking AI would already be doing planning and fault summaries, so I would ask the fitter what hands-on repairs I could learn for pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the paramedic wage would keep us fed, but it would not replace my mine income for years. I would show my partner the training offer in writing before trusting it. Three months of savings would not bridge years without a wage.

I would press for a **funded transfer** before the mine replaces operators at the belt.

feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected shift loss and a short savings bridge.
S2.quote: Three months of savings would not bridge years without a wage.
fieldNote: She identifies **2028 thinking work** in planning and logs, with the main wage threat from 2031 robots.
Her **three-month reserve** cannot cover years away from work, so a funded transfer matters immediately.

steps.text: Ask the plant manager which stacker tests retain operators
Apply for fitter training if mine fees and wages are covered
Bring a paid-transfer demand to the union committee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2031 thinking AI changes planning while the stacker remains hands-on until robots around 2034. I would ask for paid fitter places before the first operator roster is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, I could finish a fitter course while drawing plant wages. At 66 in 2034, I might still need work; the extra time is useful only if a workshop post opens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enroll in the mine-paid fitter course if my shift wages continue. I'd keep running the stacker in 2032 while logging repairs with the fitter. I'd apply for a workshop vacancy once the course qualifies me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to test whether I actually like repair work. I would still be anxious about the robot date until a workshop vacancy was real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What repair would you learn first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with the bent guide plate on the wet-ore chute, because I watched the fitter straighten it. I know the symptom; I need to learn the safe method and the measurement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the workshop has no opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep stacker shifts while I apply at the other mines, even if that means a longer commute. I would not spend our retirement reserve waiting beside a certificate.

fieldNote: She chooses **guide-plate repair** as a concrete first skill tied to a known stacker fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2036 thinking AI may handle plant plans while robots reach the stacker around 2039. I would tell the crew a decade of warning needs real funded places, even for older operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I may want fewer shifts, but I will measure that against our bills. By 71 in 2039, I hope to leave the stacker, though I cannot assume a pension covers everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid stacker shifts while I am fit and the belt still needs an operator. I'd transfer half my weekend premiums into our retirement account each month. I'd review retirement income with my partner each year before promising to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The long warning lets me plan without rushing to the first course. I am uneasy about my body doing night shifts at 68, but I expect the next few years' wages to remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 2037 look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 69 and might still run the stacker for paid shifts, or work in the workshop if I qualified. Thinking AI could plan the pile, but capable hands-on robots would still be about two years away in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help you retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own jobs and rent, and I would not build our plan around their income. We could ask them to visit more often, but the bills stay with my partner and me. I would not build our retirement plan around our grown children's income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because robots could reach our stacker by 2031 while I still need paid work. A funded fitter course linked to a workshop opening would help, with the union checking who gets a place.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should ask who gets the first chance to train. If the mine chooses only the youngest workers, a decade of warning will not help operators like me.

headlineQuote: If the mine chooses only the youngest workers, a decade of warning will not help operators like me.
portrait: Esther is a **58-year-old stacker operator** at a large mine, with typical pay and a vocational certificate.
Her partner's paramedic wage and **three months saved** give the household some room to absorb a short disruption.
She uses **AI daily** for fault logs but still walks the belt and checks repairs in person.
She seeks **funded fitter training** and union oversight if robot stackers threaten her shifts.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** because robot stackers around 2031 could end her paid shifts before retirement.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **funded fitter training** linked to a workshop opening, with the union checking access.
